newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Hu optimistic on economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Hu optimistic on economic outlook.

text.p: Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Friday he was cautiously optimistic about the city-state's 1997 economic outlook, and he expected it to improve with a recovery in the electronics sector.
"The outlook for 1997 is cautiously optimistic," Hu said in his budget speech for fiscal year 1997/98 at Parliament.
He said that although growth in first quarter of 1997 remained subdued at 3.8 percent, this was partly due to the high base in the first quarter last year.
Hu said the semiconductor industry appeared to have turned around, helped by rising orders from the United States.

Inventories of electronic components in the United States have been run down while new orders have risen by a healthy 17 percent in the first five months of 1997, Hu said, citing recent figures from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
"With some exceptions, the regional economies remain healthy and are expected to improve with the recovery in the global electronics industry," Hu said.
The minister said that given these factors the Ministry of Trade and Industry retains its economic growth forecast this year at between five and seven percent.
Electronics account for nearly 60 percent of exports and slower growth in the sector last year has been the main reason for Singapore's sluggish economic growth.
Hu said the economic slowdown in 1996, after three years of above-potential growth, eases the pressure of high growth but has not adversely affected the country's economic fundamentals.
He said foreign investment was forthcoming, underlining confidence in Singapore's sound economy.
Investors committed a record Singapore $8.1 billion in manufacturing investments in 1996, a 19-percent rise over 1995.
The minister said the recent economic slowdown serves as a sober and timely reminder of the city state's vulnerability as a small country which is heavily dependent on world trade.
"We have no choice but to stay internationally competitive and trim, even during boom periods when opportunities are plentiful," Hu said.
He said this meant that Singapore will have the resilience to weather bad times and use the respite to consolidate the economy, preparing to rebound when market conditions change.
